sources.title: Common pitfalls in statistical analysis: Odds versus risk
sources.publisher: Wolters Kluwer - Medknow (Perspectives in Clinical Research)
sources.locator: Definitions of risk as the chance of the outcome of interest over all possible outcomes, and of odds as the probability of an event divided by the probability of it not occurring; the passage showing risk and odds converging as an event becomes rarer; the definitions of relative risk and the odds ratio; the statement that the odds ratio differs little from relative risk when the outcome is rare, typically below 10 per cent, and is not interchangeable with it when the outcome is common

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the definitions of risk, odds, relative risk, and the odds ratio, the conversion between risk and odds, and the conditions under which the odds ratio approximates or exceeds the risk ratio. No wording, notation, table, figure, or example from the paper is reused; the paper's own clinical example is not reproduced, adapted, or re-skinned, and every table and count in this lesson is invented.

sources.title: Common pitfalls in statistical analysis: Absolute risk reduction, relative risk reduction, and number needed to treat
sources.publisher: Wolters Kluwer - Medknow (Perspectives in Clinical Research)
sources.locator: Definition of absolute risk reduction as the difference in event rates between the compared groups; relative risk reduction as that difference taken as a proportion of the control-group risk; the illustration that one 50 per cent relative reduction can mean an absolute reduction of 40 percentage points or of 1, depending on baseline risk; the reported overestimation of efficacy given in relative terms; the number needed to treat as the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the definitions of absolute and relative risk reduction, the dependence of an absolute reduction on the baseline risk for a fixed relative reduction, the reported tendency to overestimate effects presented relatively, and the reciprocal relation between the absolute risk reduction and the number needed to treat. The paper's clinical example and its numbers are not reproduced or adapted; the two programmes, the trial, and every count in this lesson were constructed independently.

sources.title: The Number Needed to Treat: 25 Years of Trials and Tribulations in Clinical Research
sources.publisher: Rambam Health Care Campus (Rambam Maimonides Medical Journal)
sources.version: Volume 6, issue 3, article e0033; DOI 10.5041/RMMJ.10218; PMID 26241223; PMCID PMC4524406
sources.locator: Passages defining the number needed to treat as the number of patients who must receive the intervention to prevent one outcome, computed as the inverse of the absolute risk reduction from cumulative incidences over a stated follow-up period; the statement that the measure is tied to the time period over which the outcome is counted; the parallel measure for adverse effects, the number needed to harm; the dependence of the resulting number on the underlying risk in the comparison group

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that a number needed to treat is the inverse of an absolute risk reduction computed over a specified follow-up period, that it therefore requires a stated time horizon and comparison, that it moves with the comparison group's underlying risk, and that the same arithmetic applied to an unwanted outcome is called a number needed to harm. No wording, table, figure, or worked example from the review is reproduced or adapted.

sources.title: CONSORT 2010 Explanation and Elaboration: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials
sources.version: Volume 340, article c869; DOI 10.1136/bmj.c869; PMID 20332511; PMCID PMC2844943
sources.locator: Checklist item 17b and its explanation, recommending that trials of a binary outcome present both absolute and relative effect sizes, and describing the number needed to treat as an absolute measure derived from the risk difference that helps a reader judge a result against their own patients

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that established reporting guidance for randomised trials asks for both absolute and relative effect sizes when the outcome is binary, and that the number needed to treat is treated there as an absolute measure supporting interpretation. No checklist wording, example, table, or figure is reproduced or adapted, and this lesson does not reproduce the checklist.

sources.title: Sensitivity, Specificity, and Predictive Values: Foundations, Pliabilities, and Pitfalls in Research and Practice
sources.version: Volume 5, article 307; DOI 10.3389/fpubh.2017.00307; PMID 29209603; PMCID PMC5701930
sources.locator: Definitions of sensitivity and specificity as probabilities computed solely among people known to have or known not to have the condition, and of the positive and negative predictive values as probabilities attached to a returned test result; the statement that predictive values depend on the prevalence of the target condition in the sample while sensitivity and specificity do not; the passage naming the reversal of these conditionals confusion of the inverse

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify which conditional probability each of the four diagnostic measures is, that predictive values move with the prevalence of the target condition while sensitivity and specificity are conditioned on a person's true state, and that treating one conditional as the other is the error named confusion of the inverse. No wording, analogy, example, table, or figure from the review is reused; the meter, both populations, and every count are invented.
